VIDEO.title: God Rescued Them... Then Refused to Let Them In
VIDEO.series: The Book of Hebrews, Every Word (playlist in progress)

kicker: Study aid · Hebrews 3 · Episode 4 (#4 of 4 so far in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher opens with one of the strongest warnings in the New Testament, addressed to 'holy brothers'. Why warn holy brothers about falling away, and how could what happened to a whole generation of Israel happen in our churches? He reads Hebrews 3: consider Jesus, faithful like Moses but worthy of more glory, as the builder over the house; Moses was faithful as a servant, Christ as a Son over God's house, 'whose house we are, if we hold fast'. Then Psalm 95: 'Today if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts'; take care lest an evil, unbelieving heart fall away from the living God; encourage one another daily; the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief.

Review: Hebrews 1-2 give both the greatness and the nearness of Jesus: the exalted Son who perfectly reveals God and the incarnate Savior who suffers to bring many sons to glory. The call to consider Jesus (3:1) echoes 'pay much closer attention' (2:1). The readers are identified before they are warned: holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, people inside the covenant community, not outsiders like Pontius Pilate, Nero, Richard Dawkins or Alex O'Connor. The author speaks like a pastor.

Observations: this is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle, the 'sent one' of God, who is no ordinary messenger but the Son. 'House' (oikos) means both God's covenant people and His dwelling, tabernacle and temple (compare John 2:16). 'Partakers of Christ' (3:14) and 'partakers of a heavenly calling' (3:1) describe genuine participation, tied to holding fast to the end. God's rest (3:11, 18) begins with Israel's land, but chapter 4 will take it further. The heavy Old Testament categories suggest readers of Jewish background, or at least deeply formed by Israel's Scriptures, tempted to retreat into older covenant structures as if they were enough apart from Christ.

Old Testament background: calling as holy nation and treasured possession (Exodus 19:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Genesis 12:1-3); high priest (Exodus 28-29; Leviticus 16; Psalm 110:4); 'faithful in all My household' (Numbers 12:7); God's house as sanctuary and temple (Exodus 25:8; 1 Kings 8:13; Psalm 27:4); the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18) and a provisional old covenant pointing beyond itself (Deuteronomy 30:1-14); the Son over the house (2 Samuel 7:12-14; Psalm 2:7, 12; Psalm 89:26-27); Psalm 95, a worship psalm that turns to warning; and rest from creation (Genesis 2:2) to the land (Deuteronomy 12:9), with Sabbath as a hint of where all things are headed.

Before arguments about perseverance and whether a Christian can lose salvation, which matter and have real answers, Hebrews warns a real congregation: don't harden your hearts, don't fall away, exhort one another while it is still called Today. 'Hear' in Jewish thinking includes obeying.

The lesson: 'A person can be among God's people, inside God's house, and still harden their heart against His voice.' The wilderness generation had Moses, the covenant community and God's miracles, and still hardened their hearts through unbelief.
QUOTES: A person can be among God's people, inside God's house, and still harden their heart against His voice.
He is reminding the readers of their identity before they are warned about their danger.
Hebrews is not first inviting us into a theological cage match.
Knowing the word of God well, but not being transformed by it, very often turns a person into a prideful know-it-all.

method.p: In Hebrews 3 circle every 'house', 'today', 'harden' and 'hold fast'. Then read Psalm 95 in full and note where its joyful opening turns into warning.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession—Jesus,
But encourage one another day after day, as long as it is still called “Today,” so that none of you will be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
So we see that they were not able to enter because of unbelief.

left.text: For this reason we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away.

right.text: Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession—Jesus,

lines.text: 'Therefore' builds on chapters 1-2. 'Consider' means to notice carefully and fix one's attention. To a discouraged, pressured church tempted to shrink back, the author says: pay attention, consider Jesus. And he names them holy brothers before he warns them, as a pastor would.

src.text: in these last days spoke to us in His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, through whom also He made the worlds,

lines.text: This is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle. An apostle is a sent one, and God sent Jesus. But the one sent is no ordinary messenger; He is the Son who shares God's very nature (1:3).

CONSIDER.title: A heavenly calling, a high priest

left.text: and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you shall speak to the sons of Israel.”

right.text: Yahweh has sworn and will not change His mind, / “You are a priest forever / According to the order of Melchizedek.”

lines.text: 'Holy' and 'calling' evoke Israel as God's treasured possession: 'For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God' (Deuteronomy 7:6); compare Abram's call (Genesis 12:1-3). The calling is heavenly because it comes from God and draws His people toward a heavenly inheritance. 'High priest' rests on Aaron (Exodus 28-29), the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) and Psalm 110, which Hebrews already used in 1:13.

left.text: “Not so, with My servant Moses, / He is faithful in all My household;

right.text: but Christ was faithful as a Son over His house—whose house we are, if we hold fast our confidence and the boast of our hope.

lines.text: In Numbers 12 the house is God's covenant household, Israel. Moses was faithful as a servant within it; Christ is faithful as a Son over it, as the builder has more honor than the house (3:3). The point is not merely that Jesus is greater, but that the people of His house must hold fast.

left.text: And let them make a sanctuary for Me, that I may dwell among them.

right.text: One thing I have asked from Yahweh, that I shall seek: / That I may dwell in the house of Yahweh all the days of my life, / To behold the beauty of Yahweh / And to inquire in His temple.

lines.text: Because Moses oversaw the tabernacle, 'house' also has sanctuary resonance, and later becomes temple language: 'I have surely built You a lofty house' (1 Kings 8:13). Jesus calls the temple 'My Father's house' (John 2:16). In Hebrews the house is primarily God's people, among whom He dwells.

left.text: “Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; you shall listen to him.

right.text: Kiss the Son, lest He become angry, and you perish in the way, / For His wrath may soon be kindled. / How blessed are all who take refuge in Him!

lines.text: Moses testified 'of those things which were to be spoken later' (Hebrews 3:5); Deuteronomy 18 and 30 look ahead. The old covenant was genuinely from God but provisional and preparatory. 'Son over His house' connects to royal sonship: 2 Samuel 7:12-14, Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 89:26-27.

TODAY.title: Today, if you hear His voice

left.text: Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, / As in the day of Massah in the wilderness,

right.text: So he named the place Massah and Meribah because of the contending of the sons of Israel, and because they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”

lines.text: Psalm 95 begins in joyful praise, 'Let us make a loud shout to the rock of our salvation' (Psalm 95:1), then turns sharply to warning: the same people who sang of deliverance hardened their hearts at Meribah. 'Today' (Hebrews 3:13) means every day God's people can hear or harden. In Jewish thinking, to hear includes to obey.

src.text: See to it brothers, that there not be in any one of you an evil, unbelieving heart that falls away from the living God.

lines.text: 'For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold fast the beginning of our assurance firm until the end' (Hebrews 3:14). Many readers immediately sift this through debates over election, predestination, free will and perseverance. The teacher says those conversations matter and have real answers, but asks us first to hear the warning to a real congregation.

TODAY.title: They shall not enter My rest

left.text: And on the seventh day God completed His work which He had done, and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had done.

right.text: for you have not as yet come to the resting place and the inheritance which Yahweh your God is giving you.

lines.text: God's rest is not tiredness: He ceased His creative work and entered the order and rule of what He made. Then rest becomes Israel entering the land. The Sabbath was a hint of where all things are headed. The wilderness generation fell: 'your corpses will fall in this wilderness' (Numbers 14:29). Chapter 4 says the promise still stands.

What believers openly profess about Jesus (3:1).

BACKGROUND.p: The letter never says. Its reliance on angels, the wilderness generation, Joshua, Sabbath, Aaron's priesthood, Melchizedek, the tabernacle, sacrifices, the Day of Atonement, covenant, Sinai and Zion suggests readers with a working knowledge of the Old Testament, most naturally believers of Jewish background, though Gentiles from the synagogue world also knew it well.

After the Exodus, Israel tested God at Massah and Meribah (Exodus 17) and refused to enter the land at Kadesh (Numbers 14); that generation died in the wilderness over forty years. Psalm 95 holds them up as a warning for worshipers.
Rest begins at creation's seventh day, becomes the promised land, and is marked weekly by the Sabbath. Hebrews 4 will argue that 'there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God' (Hebrews 4:9).

DEBATES.p: Some read the warning as addressed to genuine believers who could forfeit salvation; others to people who profess faith without possessing it ('partakers... if we hold fast' showing who truly belongs); others see the warnings as a means God uses to keep His people. The video declines a 'cage match' here and says the topic will return in chapter 6.
The video infers Jewish-background believers from the letter's Old Testament depth. Some scholars argue for a mixed or Gentile audience well taught in the Greek Old Testament.

Readings include the land of Canaan as a type, a present spiritual rest in Christ, and the final rest of the age to come. Chrysostom took it as the kingdom of heaven, of which the Sabbath was an image.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small points worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video quotes 'Therefore I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest' as part of Psalm 95:10; it is 95:11.
The video reads Exodus 25:8 on into 'exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle', which is 25:9.
Where Psalm 95:8 names Meribah and Massah, Hebrews 3:8, following the Greek, translates them as 'when they provoked Me' and 'the day of trial' (the names mean quarreling and testing).

QUESTIONS: Why does the author call them 'holy brothers' right before a severe warning?
What does it mean that Jesus is both Apostle and High Priest?
How can someone be inside God's house and still harden their heart?
Who are you exhorting, and who exhorts you, 'day after day'?
Where might familiarity with Scripture be keeping you from being softened by it?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The teacher knows this lesson all too well. He grew up in a family that served faithfully every week: Sunday morning and evening, setup and teardown, Tuesday fellowship, Wednesday service, youth group, rehearsals, church plays; his father was a musician on the worship team, his mother a dancer and choreographer. At five he prayed the sinner's prayer with his mother in her prayer closet to please her. He memorized the books of the Bible and knew the gospel, but he wasn't saved. At 17 he told his parents he wasn't going back, fed up with perceived hypocrisy and rules he refused to obey; God looked like a cold prison warden because his heart was hard. Many people can know the language, doctrine and arguments of Scripture and still not be softened by God's voice; knowing it without being transformed tends to make a prideful know-it-all. Only by God's mercy, who came and got him, is he in God's family today. That's why he serves in prisons, why he loves his friend and pastor Robby Gallaty's heart for this, why he teaches apologetics to adults and the next generation, and why he speaks to churches, where he often sees people raised in church who say the right things outwardly but are inwardly unmoved. 'Exhort one another every day as long as it is called today.'
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): read Psalm 95 aloud as a prayer, then name one person you will encourage this week while it is still called Today.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher opens with one of the strongest warnings in the New Testament, addressed to 'holy brothers'. Why warn holy brothers about falling away, and how could what happened to a whole generation of Israel happen in our churches? He reads Hebrews 3: consider Jesus, faithful like Moses but worthy of more glory, as the builder over the house; Moses was faithful as a servant, Christ as a Son over God's house, 'whose house we are, if we hold fast'. Then Psalm 95: 'Today if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts'; take care lest an evil, unbelieving heart fall away from the living God; encourage one another daily; the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief.
- Review: Hebrews 1-2 give both the greatness and the nearness of Jesus: the exalted Son who perfectly reveals God and the incarnate Savior who suffers to bring many sons to glory. The call to consider Jesus (3:1) echoes 'pay much closer attention' (2:1). The readers are identified before they are warned: holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, people inside the covenant community, not outsiders like Pontius Pilate, Nero, Richard Dawkins or Alex O'Connor. The author speaks like a pastor.
- Observations: this is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle, the 'sent one' of God, who is no ordinary messenger but the Son. 'House' (oikos) means both God's covenant people and His dwelling, tabernacle and temple (compare John 2:16). 'Partakers of Christ' (3:14) and 'partakers of a heavenly calling' (3:1) describe genuine participation, tied to holding fast to the end. God's rest (3:11, 18) begins with Israel's land, but chapter 4 will take it further. The heavy Old Testament categories suggest readers of Jewish background, or at least deeply formed by Israel's Scriptures, tempted to retreat into older covenant structures as if they were enough apart from Christ.
- Old Testament background: calling as holy nation and treasured possession (Exodus 19:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Genesis 12:1-3); high priest (Exodus 28-29; Leviticus 16; Psalm 110:4); 'faithful in all My household' (Numbers 12:7); God's house as sanctuary and temple (Exodus 25:8; 1 Kings 8:13; Psalm 27:4); the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18) and a provisional old covenant pointing beyond itself (Deuteronomy 30:1-14); the Son over the house (2 Samuel 7:12-14; Psalm 2:7, 12; Psalm 89:26-27); Psalm 95, a worship psalm that turns to warning; and rest from creation (Genesis 2:2) to the land (Deuteronomy 12:9), with Sabbath as a hint of where all things are headed.
- Before arguments about perseverance and whether a Christian can lose salvation, which matter and have real answers, Hebrews warns a real congregation: don't harden your hearts, don't fall away, exhort one another while it is still called Today. 'Hear' in Jewish thinking includes obeying.
- The lesson: 'A person can be among God's people, inside God's house, and still harden their heart against His voice.' The wilderness generation had Moses, the covenant community and God's miracles, and still hardened their hearts through unbelief.

## Consider Jesus
1. Hebrews 3:1; 2:1: Consider Jesus
   Hebrews (Hebrews 2:1, LSB): "For this reason we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away."
   Hebrews (Hebrews 3:1, LSB): "Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession—Jesus,"
   (video) 'Therefore' builds on chapters 1-2. 'Consider' means to notice carefully and fix one's attention. To a discouraged, pressured church tempted to shrink back, the author says: pay attention, consider Jesus. And he names them holy brothers before he warns them, as a pastor would.
2. Hebrews 3:1; 1:2: The Apostle
   The sent one of God Hebrews 1:2: "in these last days spoke to us in His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, through whom also He made the worlds," https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Hebrews+1:2
   (video) This is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle. An apostle is a sent one, and God sent Jesus. But the one sent is no ordinary messenger; He is the Son who shares God's very nature (1:3).
3. Hebrews 3:1; Exodus 19:5-6; Psalm 110:4: A heavenly calling, a high priest
   Moses (Exodus 19:6, LSB): "and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you shall speak to the sons of Israel.”"
   David (Psalm 110:4, LSB): "Yahweh has sworn and will not change His mind, / “You are a priest forever / According to the order of Melchizedek.”"
   (video) 'Holy' and 'calling' evoke Israel as God's treasured possession: 'For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God' (Deuteronomy 7:6); compare Abram's call (Genesis 12:1-3). The calling is heavenly because it comes from God and draws His people toward a heavenly inheritance. 'High priest' rests on Aaron (Exodus 28-29), the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) and Psalm 110, which Hebrews already used in 1:13. (Deuteronomy 7:6)

## Whose house we are
1. Hebrews 3:2-5; Numbers 12:7: Faithful in all His house
   Yahweh (Numbers 12:7, LSB): "“Not so, with My servant Moses, / He is faithful in all My household;"
   Hebrews (Hebrews 3:6, LSB): "but Christ was faithful as a Son over His house—whose house we are, if we hold fast our confidence and the boast of our hope."
   (video) In Numbers 12 the house is God's covenant household, Israel. Moses was faithful as a servant within it; Christ is faithful as a Son over it, as the builder has more honor than the house (3:3). The point is not merely that Jesus is greater, but that the people of His house must hold fast.
2. Exodus 25:8; 1 Kings 8:13; Psalm 27:4: House as sanctuary
   Moses (Exodus 25:8, LSB): "And let them make a sanctuary for Me, that I may dwell among them."
   David (Psalm 27:4, LSB): "One thing I have asked from Yahweh, that I shall seek: / That I may dwell in the house of Yahweh all the days of my life, / To behold the beauty of Yahweh / And to inquire in His temple."
   (video) Because Moses oversaw the tabernacle, 'house' also has sanctuary resonance, and later becomes temple language: 'I have surely built You a lofty house' (1 Kings 8:13). Jesus calls the temple 'My Father's house' (John 2:16). In Hebrews the house is primarily God's people, among whom He dwells. (1 Kings 8:13; John 2:16)
3. Hebrews 3:5-6; Deuteronomy 18:15; Psalm 2:12: Testimony and the Son
   Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15, LSB): "“Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; you shall listen to him."
   David (Psalm 2:12, LSB): "Kiss the Son, lest He become angry, and you perish in the way, / For His wrath may soon be kindled. / How blessed are all who take refuge in Him!"
   (video) Moses testified 'of those things which were to be spoken later' (Hebrews 3:5); Deuteronomy 18 and 30 look ahead. The old covenant was genuinely from God but provisional and preparatory. 'Son over His house' connects to royal sonship: 2 Samuel 7:12-14, Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 89:26-27. (Hebrews 3:5)

## Today, if you hear His voice
1. Hebrews 3:7-11; Psalm 95:7-8; Exodus 17:7: Today, if you hear His voice
   Psalmist (Psalm 95:8, LSB): "Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, / As in the day of Massah in the wilderness,"
   Moses (Exodus 17:7, LSB): "So he named the place Massah and Meribah because of the contending of the sons of Israel, and because they tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”"
   (video) Psalm 95 begins in joyful praise, 'Let us make a loud shout to the rock of our salvation' (Psalm 95:1), then turns sharply to warning: the same people who sang of deliverance hardened their hearts at Meribah. 'Today' (Hebrews 3:13) means every day God's people can hear or harden. In Jewish thinking, to hear includes to obey. (Psalm 95:1)
2. Hebrews 3:12-14: An evil, unbelieving heart
   Exhort one another Hebrews 3:12: "See to it brothers, that there not be in any one of you an evil, unbelieving heart that falls away from the living God." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Hebrews+3:12
   (video) 'For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold fast the beginning of our assurance firm until the end' (Hebrews 3:14). Many readers immediately sift this through debates over election, predestination, free will and perseverance. The teacher says those conversations matter and have real answers, but asks us first to hear the warning to a real congregation. (Hebrews 3:14)
3. Hebrews 3:16-19; Genesis 2:2; Deuteronomy 12:9: They shall not enter My rest
   Moses (Genesis 2:2, LSB): "And on the seventh day God completed His work which He had done, and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had done."
   Moses (Deuteronomy 12:9, LSB): "for you have not as yet come to the resting place and the inheritance which Yahweh your God is giving you."
   (video) God's rest is not tiredness: He ceased His creative work and entered the order and rule of what He made. Then rest becomes Israel entering the land. The Sabbath was a hint of where all things are headed. The wilderness generation fell: 'your corpses will fall in this wilderness' (Numbers 14:29). Chapter 4 says the promise still stands. (Numbers 14:29)

## Key people
- Moses: Faithful in all God's house as a servant, testifying to what was to be spoken later (3:2, 5). [Background] Numbers 12:7 is the source of the phrase.
- The wilderness generation: Saw God's works for forty years, yet provoked Him and could not enter because of unbelief (3:9, 16-19). [Background] Numbers 14 records their refusal at Kadesh.
- Melchizedek: The order of the forever priest in Psalm 110:4. [Background] Priest-king of Salem (Genesis 14:18); Hebrews 5-7 develops him.
- Joshua: Among the Old Testament categories the letter assumes its readers know. [Background] He led Israel into the land; Hebrews 4:8 says he did not give them the final rest.
- David: Psalms 2, 27, 89 and 110 are cited; Hebrews 4:7 credits Psalm 95 to David. [Background] 'saying through David after so long a time' (Hebrews 4:7).
- Pontius Pilate: Named as an example of an outsider the warning is not addressed to. [Background] Roman governor who sentenced Jesus.

## Places [Background]
- Egypt (named in the video): 'All those who came out of Egypt led by Moses' (3:16).
- Massah and Meribah (named in the video): Where Israel tested Yahweh (Exodus 17:7; Psalm 95:8). Traditionally placed at Rephidim; approximate.
- Mount Sinai: Where Israel became God's covenant people (Exodus 19). Traditional site.
- Kadesh-barnea: Where the generation refused to enter the land (Numbers 13-14). Approximate.

## Key terms
- Apostle: 'Sent one'; Jesus is the one God sent (3:1).
- Confession: What believers openly profess about Jesus (3:1).
- House (oikos): God's covenant household and His dwelling: tabernacle, temple, His people (3:2-6).
- Rest: God's completed rule and presence: creation's seventh day, the land, and more (3:11).
- Perseverance of the saints: The doctrine that true believers continue to the end; much debated in Hebrews 3 and 6.
- Inference: An educated guess from evidence, such as who the readers were.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Who were the readers?: The letter never says. Its reliance on angels, the wilderness generation, Joshua, Sabbath, Aaron's priesthood, Melchizedek, the tabernacle, sacrifices, the Day of Atonement, covenant, Sinai and Zion suggests readers with a working knowledge of the Old Testament, most naturally believers of Jewish background, though Gentiles from the synagogue world also knew it well.
- The wilderness generation: After the Exodus, Israel tested God at Massah and Meribah (Exodus 17) and refused to enter the land at Kadesh (Numbers 14); that generation died in the wilderness over forty years. Psalm 95 holds them up as a warning for worshipers.
- Rest and Sabbath: Rest begins at creation's seventh day, becomes the promised land, and is marked weekly by the Sabbath. Hebrews 4 will argue that 'there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God' (Hebrews 4:9).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 400): "For from hardness unbelief arises: and as in bodies, the parts that have become callous and hard do not yield to the hands of the physicians, so also souls that are hardened yield not to the word of God." Homilies on Hebrews 6, on 3:12. NPNF 1.14 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 400): "Since to them also is this word addressed: for, Today (he says) is ever, so long as the world lasts." Homilies on Hebrews 6, on 3:12-13. NPNF 1.14 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 400): "What other rest then is there, except the kingdom of Heaven, of which the Sabbath was an image and type?" Homilies on Hebrews 6, on 3:7-11. NPNF 1.14 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Can a Christian fall away? (3:12-14) Some read the warning as addressed to genuine believers who could forfeit salvation; others to people who profess faith without possessing it ('partakers... if we hold fast' showing who truly belongs); others see the warnings as a means God uses to keep His people. The video declines a 'cage match' here and says the topic will return in chapter 6.
- Jewish or Gentile readers? The video infers Jewish-background believers from the letter's Old Testament depth. Some scholars argue for a mixed or Gentile audience well taught in the Greek Old Testament.
- What is God's rest? Readings include the land of Canaan as a type, a present spiritual rest in Christ, and the final rest of the age to come. Chrysostom took it as the kingdom of heaven, of which the Sabbath was an image.

## Careful reading notes
Small points worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video quotes 'Therefore I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest' as part of Psalm 95:10; it is 95:11.
- The video reads Exodus 25:8 on into 'exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle', which is 25:9.
- Where Psalm 95:8 names Meribah and Massah, Hebrews 3:8, following the Greek, translates them as 'when they provoked Me' and 'the day of trial' (the names mean quarreling and testing).

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why does the author call them 'holy brothers' right before a severe warning?
2. What does it mean that Jesus is both Apostle and High Priest?
3. How can someone be inside God's house and still harden their heart?
4. Who are you exhorting, and who exhorts you, 'day after day'?
5. Where might familiarity with Scripture be keeping you from being softened by it?

## Application
- (video) The teacher knows this lesson all too well. He grew up in a family that served faithfully every week: Sunday morning and evening, setup and teardown, Tuesday fellowship, Wednesday service, youth group, rehearsals, church plays; his father was a musician on the worship team, his mother a dancer and choreographer. At five he prayed the sinner's prayer with his mother in her prayer closet to please her. He memorized the books of the Bible and knew the gospel, but he wasn't saved. At 17 he told his parents he wasn't going back, fed up with perceived hypocrisy and rules he refused to obey; God looked like a cold prison warden because his heart was hard. Many people can know the language, doctrine and arguments of Scripture and still not be softened by God's voice; knowing it without being transformed tends to make a prideful know-it-all. Only by God's mercy, who came and got him, is he in God's family today. That's why he serves in prisons, why he loves his friend and pastor Robby Gallaty's heart for this, why he teaches apologetics to adults and the next generation, and why he speaks to churches, where he often sees people raised in church who say the right things outwardly but are inwardly unmoved. 'Exhort one another every day as long as it is called today.'
- Study note (added): read Psalm 95 aloud as a prayer, then name one person you will encourage this week while it is still called Today.
